Article Title: 'Too deferential to govt': Former SC judge questions ex-CJI Chandrachud’s approach to appointments
Article Text:
Congress flags judicial independence concerns over claims in ex SC judge's memoir

Congress flags judicial independence concerns

NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has questioned former Chief Justice of India (CJI) D Y Chandrachud's approach to judicial appointments, alleging that he was "too deferential to the government". He also expressed concern over the practice of discussing candidates with the executive before formal Collegium deliberations.In his forthcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, Justice Kaul recounts a Collegium meeting to fill six vacancies in the Supreme Court, during which five names had been agreed upon in advance. He alleges that Justice Chandrachud proposed a sixth candidate at the last minute and considered seeking the government's view on the appointment."The Chief Justice drew me aside into a separate room and wondered aloud whether he should telephone out to check the government's view," Kaul wrote in his book.Speaking to news portal The Wire about his memoir, Kaul said the Collegium must resist executive pressure to safeguard judicial independence.Asked whether Justice Chandrachud was trying to please the government or seeking its prior approval, Kaul said, "I don't think it was a question of pleasing the government, but what had happened was that he had discussed the names with me earlier."We had agreed on five names, and I thought the collegium would be quite okay with the other members of the collegium, and this (sixth) name was propped up at the last minute with me while going to the collegium meeting. I said that name is not acceptable to me and will not be acceptable."He said Justice Chandrachud wanted him to support the additional candidate, but he believed the other Collegium members would also oppose the proposal."And well, he wanted me to collaborate and go ahead with the name. I said even if I do that, the others will not. I believe, and that's what happened in the meeting. I told him this will not get through because I know the views of the other collegiate members. Maybe he had already taken some kind of an approval for the other names, including the sixth name," Kaul said.He expressed concern over the practice of discussing judicial appointments with the government before formal Collegium meetings."So this has become, unfortunately, a practice of names being discussed in some kind of a previous discussion with the government," he told senior journalist Karan Thapar."It has been happening, I think, before and after, which is what troubles me. That's why I have written that when the government introduced the NJAC (the National Judicial Appointments Commission) in 2015, we would at least have sat across the table and discussed it. It could have been fine-tuned. It could be modulated," Kaul said.Justice Kaul, who retired in December 2023, wrote that differences over how to deal with the executive strained his relationship with Justice Chandrachud, under whom he served on the Collegium from June 2022."There is a difference between consultation and what I came to regard as pre-approval, seeking the government's nod before the collegium had even formally deliberated," Kaul wrote in his memoir.Explaining why he considered Justice Chandrachud "too deferential to the government on appointment matters," Kaul said the practice could create difficulties for future Chief Justices, particularly those with shorter tenures."Well, he believed that this is how it had been happening, and I was of the view that you, with a chief justice like you, and with two years' tenure, and with your own merit and the trust, if you do this, the successors would have a problem in not following this practice because they have shorter tenures.""And the government would get used to a particular methodology before appointments to the Supreme Court were made, and that's why I endeavoured to discourage him from discussing everything beforehand," Kaul said.The former judge also raised objections to the transfer of a case concerning the reconsideration of certain aspects of a Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) judgment from a bench headed by him to another bench. He argued that cases should not be reassigned because of apprehensions about how a particular bench might decide them.The Congress on Sunday raised concerns over the independence of the judiciary under the Narendra Modi government, citing revelations in the forthcoming memoir. The party asserted that the institution responsible for upholding the Constitution must remain free from pressure exerted by those in power.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report quoting the pre-publication manuscript of Kaul's memoir, Without Fear of Favour, which reportedly states that Chief Justice of India (CJI) Justice D Y Chandrachud was "too deferential to the Government" on judicial appointments.In a post on X, Ramesh said, "A book by former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has raised serious questions regarding the independence of the judiciary during the tenure of the Modi government."Ramesh said Kaul had highlighted several concerning incidents, including alleged government interference in judicial appointments, attempts to secure government approval before Collegium meetings and the government's questioning of the caste of a judge belonging to a minority community.He added that issues many had previously been hesitant to discuss openly had now been documented by Kaul in measured and deliberate language."Strikingly, a former Chief Justice of India (CJI) has not denied that discussions with the government take place prior to judicial appointments. When former CJI Justice Chandrachud acknowledges that the government engages with the CJI and plays a role in the appointment process, the concerns surrounding judicial independence become even more profound," Ramesh said.The Congress leader also flagged Kaul's account of an incident involving a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). According to Ramesh, Kaul revealed that after a bench presided over by him raised the possibility of reconsidering certain aspects of a court ruling in the case, the matter was reassigned to another bench without consulting him."This points to the extent of the government's day-to-day interference in the functioning of the Supreme Court," Ramesh said.Questioning the implications of the alleged incidents, he said, "When there is pressure to obtain government approval for judicial appointments, and when benches hearing sensitive cases are altered, one must ask -- in the interest of safeguarding democracy -- if this does not constitute pressure on the judiciary and an erosion of its independence, then what does?"Emphasising the importance of judicial independence in a democracy, Ramesh said, "The institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power. In a democracy, the independence of the judiciary is not merely an option; it is an absolute necessity," Ramesh asserted.
Article Summary: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has questioned former Chief Justice of India D Y Chandrachud's approach to judicial appointments. He alleges that he was "too deferential to the government" He also expressed concern over the practice of discussing candidates with the executive before formal Collegium deliberations. Congress flags judicial independence concerns over claims in ex SC judge's memoir.

Article Title: Give mayors real powers, ensure timely civic audits, urban body heads tell Centre
Article Text:
National Urban Enclave 2026

NEW DELHI: Even as the Centre moots directly elected mayors with a fixed five-year tenure and a mayor-in-council system, municipal heads from different cities at National Urban Conclave flagged that the move would serve little purpose without giving mayors adequate powers. Rajkot mayor Nehal Shukla also called for time-bound financial audits of civic bodies, saying that “no municipal body can function without financial irregularities”.Participating in a discussion on proposed changes to the Model Municipal Law, Shukla said mayors in municipal governance were like governors, while standing committees wielded financial powers and executive officials remained under the control of state govts.“Wherever we have directly elected mayors, we must have a mayor-in-council. If you don’t give power to the mayor, direct election hardly serves any objective,” he said.Under the mayor-in-Council system, executive powers to run a city on a day-to-day basis are shared between the mayor and a small, cabinet-like group of elected councillors, who are individually accountable for their respective portfolios.Shukla also suggested that municipal elections be conducted by the Election Commission, citing its track record of holding timely general and assembly elections.He said state govts invariably found one reason or another to delay municipal polls.“The biggest missing thing that needs to be fixed is timely audits to bring financial discipline. Audit reports are delayed by six to eight years, and that’s why irregularities do not come to light. We all know that no municipal body can function without financial irregularities,” he said.Shukla pointed out that rules require tenders to be floated for works or services costing more than Rs 5 lakh, but alleged that this was often not followed. Municipal commissioners, he said, were aware of such violations but approved the transactions because otherwise civic bodies could not function.He suggested that audits be conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). If state auditors continued to conduct them, he said, the law should ensure that the audit backlog did not exceed two years.Bhubaneswar mayor Sulochana Das, who also participated in the discussion, said municipal laws were robust on paper, but the ground reality was different.“People have more expectations from directly elected mayors. But we have no power. Executive officers such as municipal commissioners are beyond the control of mayors, as we cannot write their annual performance reports or have any say in their appointments. Commissioners change frequently,” she said.
Article Summary: The Centre moots directly elected mayors with a fixed five-year tenure. Rajkot mayor Nehal Shukla also called for time-bound financial audits of civic bodies. He suggested that audits be conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)

Article Title: 'Now that Nitish is no longer there': Expelled Anant Singh says has no regrets, to float own party

NEW DELHI: Expelled Janata Dal (United) strongman Anant Singh on Sunday claimed the Nitish Kumar 's party is “finished” after his expulsion, predicting that it would fail to win even 10 seats in the next election.The Mokama MLA and Nitish Kumar loyalist also said he had “no regrets” over the action and maintained that he shared a cordial relationship with Nitish Kumar.Anant Singh's remarks came a day after the JD(U), which has been in power in Bihar for nearly two decades under Nitish Kumar’s leadership, expelled him and his wife, Neelam Devi , for six years over alleged “anti-party” activities.Speaking to reporters, Singh said he would form his own political party and questioned the future of the JD(U) after Nitish Kumar’s exit from Bihar throne and move away from an active role in state politics.“The party belonged to Nitish Kumar. Now that Nitish Kumar is no longer there (in the active role), what is left of the party? Who among those in the leadership-- the ones who expelled me—has actually contributed anything?... Now, they will not even get 10 seats... Why will I go anywhere? I will simply build my own party,” he said.“The JD(U) is finished. Once they hold elections, everything will become clear,” Mokama MLA added.Despite his criticism of the party, Singh denied any rift with Nitish Kumar, saying, “There is no distance between me and Nitish-ji; we maintain a cordial relationship. I will go and visit him sometime -- there’s no issue. Let them keep their party; it serves no real purpose anyway.”“I will simply build my own party... I have no regrets. Whatever action has been taken, it’s fine; I have no issues with it,” he said.The JD(U) had accused Anant Singh of repeatedly disobeying the party leadership and using inappropriate and insulting language against its senior leaders.In a further move, the party has approached Bihar Legislative Assembly Speaker Prem Kumar seeking Singh’s disqualification as an MLA under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, commonly known as the anti-defection law.

JAMMU: A suspicious pigeon carrying a coded ring, a chit written in Urdu and Pakistani currency was caught by locals along the border in Jammu’s Samba district on Saturday, officials said.An official pointed out that such episodes are not uncommon in border areas of J&K and Punjab, where pigeons have been used for smuggling or for sending messages across the frontier.On Saturday, the pigeon was found near a temple in Samba’s border area of Mawa around 6.40am and was immediately captured by locals after they spotted a ring tied to its leg. “A ring bearing Code No 03341214150 was found attached to its leg, besides the note and currency,” the official said.A police team arrived soon and seized the pigeon with the items. “The pigeon has been taken for examination. On Oct 17, a suspicious aircraft-shaped balloon bearing the PIA symbol was seized from Jammu’s Khaur area.

Article Title: Presidential election today? Trump confuses India with Brazil, claims 125 million voted
Article Text:
Trump says "125 million Indians voted in presidential election today."

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian "presidential election" He also questioned the integrity of the American voting system. India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college.

Article Title: 99 runs leaked in 2 T20Is! Bhuvneshwar Kumar gets a message from Morne Morkel
Article Text:

Morkel backs Bhuvneshwar to find his rhythm

India bowling coach Morne Morkel has asked Bhuvneshwar Kumar to stay calm, ignore outside pressure and focus on his own game as the experienced fast bowler tries to find his rhythm after returning to the T20I team following a four-year gap.Bhuvneshwar's comeback has not gone as planned. The 36-year-old conceded 49 runs in the first T20I against New Zealand and 50 in the second, taking just one wicket across the two matches. His economy rate of 12.37 has been the highest among India's bowlers in the series.With India leading 2-0 in the five-match series, Morkel has backed the veteran pacer to improve as he gets more opportunities on the field.Morkel said Bhuvneshwar would naturally face expectations after returning to the international stage following four years away from the T20I side. He also pointed to the bowler's strong performances in the IPL."I've got a lot of sympathy for his return. There will be expectations after four years to come back. He has done exceptionally well in the IPL and bowled really well," Morkel said on the eve of the third T20I.The bowling coach said preparing for international cricket was not easy, especially when a player had limited time to get ready before the series."One challenge is to block the expectation factor out. Two, leading into selection, he trained for a month, but playing international cricket is a different beast where the margins are small.He had to come in with limited training because of the schedule to get himself ready."Bhuvneshwar played an important role in Royal Challengers Bengaluru's back-to-back IPL titles. He took 17 wickets in the 2025 season and followed that up with 28 wickets in 2026.Despite the expensive outings in the first two matches, Morkel believes Bhuvneshwar has the skills and experience needed to bounce back. He urged the bowler not to put himself under pressure to deliver immediately."The skill and his experience, everything is there. But at the end of the day, we have to respect the game of cricket and you have to be able to allow him to just find his feet in some of the games."Morkel said his message to Bhuvneshwar had been simple from the moment the pacer joined the squad."And for me, that has been the message from the start when he joined the squad, don't chase anything. Just be you."He added that the bowler should focus on his game rather than worry about what others expected from him."Yes, there will be expectations. But every game you'll get better and every game you'll find your rhythm. So let's not think about any outside noises. Just be you and connect with that," the South African added.
Article Summary: Morkel backs Bhuvneshwar to find his rhythm in T20I series against New Zealand. India bowling coach says bowler should ignore outside pressure and focus on his own game. Bhuvi has struggled since returning to India's T20 team after four years.

The quarterback has invested in several businesses and sports teams while learning how to manage his money for the future. Two people have played different roles in shaping that approach: his godfather, former MLB pitcher LaTroy Hawkins, and his teammate and close friend Travis Kelce . While Hawkins taught Mahomes about financial responsibility, Kelce showed him the value of staying open to new opportunities.In a May 2024 interview with Boardroom, Mahomes discussed the lessons he has picked up while building his business portfolio. His comments offered a look at how advice from people close to him has influenced his decisions away from the field.Mahomes learned about professional sports long before he entered the NFL. His father, Pat Mahomes, played professional baseball, and his godfather LaTroy Hawkins spent 21 seasons in Major League Baseball. Hawkins also worked in the Minnesota Twins' front office after his playing career.Having people around him who understood professional sports helped Mahomes learn that a successful career requires more than talent.Hawkins guided him on professionalism and managing money, encouraging him to think about his financial future instead of focusing only on what he earned during his playing years.Mahomes also learned about saving money from his time around locker rooms. Despite becoming the 10th overall pick in the 2017 NFL Draft, he did not buy a car until his second contract. A local marketing deal provided him with a vehicle after the Chiefs selected him.That decision reflected the financial habits he had started developing early in his career. Rather than spending quickly after entering the league, Mahomes wanted to understand how to manage his earnings.In the Boardroom interview, he explained how education and experience shaped his investment decisions.“I think it all comes with education. I’ve learned from things I’ve done in the past, finding the positives and negatives and learning from people that I have around me, and then trying to be better in the next investment or product I endorse.”Mahomes has since built a portfolio that includes stakes in the Kansas City Royals, Kansas City Current and Sporting Kansas City, alongside his wife, Brittany. His investments also extend to companies and brands outside traditional team ownership.The quarterback has made it clear that he wants to understand the opportunities he takes rather than simply attach his name to a business. His experience with Hawkins helped him recognise the value of learning before making financial decisions.Travis Kelce has also influenced how Mahomes approaches business. The two Kansas City Chiefs stars have developed a close friendship while building careers that extend beyond the NFL.Mahomes has watched Kelce expand his profile through commercial appearances, investments and other ventures. Their connection also reaches the business world, with both players investing in Alpine's Formula 1 team.Speaking about Kelce's development outside football, Mahomes said he was impressed by how his teammate had expanded his role.“He’s someone who’s expanded his role from off the football field to the status that he has now, including investments.”Mahomes also praised Kelce for carefully considering opportunities before making decisions. He said:“He does a great job of listening to every opportunity and then making the right decisions for himself.”The Chiefs quarterback also pushed back against the idea that Kelce's public image tells the whole story about him. While Kelce is known for his outgoing personality, Mahomes sees a thoughtful businessman behind it.“I always joke around that he puts on this persona that he’s this guy that just likes to party, go out, and have fun. But when he comes down to it, man, he’s a very smart dude that has done a lot of great things with his career on and off the field. That’s why he’s in the place that he’s at now.”Those observations reflect the lesson Mahomes has taken from watching his teammate. Staying open to opportunities can help athletes build careers and income streams that continue after they stop playing.Mahomes has applied that thinking to his own investments. In May 2024, he became the lead investor in Throne Sport Coffee, working with former BodyArmor executive Michael Fedele. He had taken a hands-on approach to the business, including testing four iced coffee flavours and attending meetings during the previous NFL season.His interest in the company went beyond endorsement work. He wanted to be involved in the product and understand the business he was supporting.Mahomes has also explained why he takes a long-term view of his finances. He said:“I’m trying to provide for not only myself now but my kids and then their families as well.”He added that saving and choosing the right people to work with are important parts of that plan.“So, you’ve got to save your money and invest in good people like Michael and Throne Sport Coffee, and hopefully, that money can multiply.”Hawkins helped Mahomes understand the importance of financial discipline, while Kelce offered an example of how athletes can grow their presence beyond sports. Together, their influence has helped Mahomes approach business with a focus on learning, careful decisions and building a future for his family.
Article Summary: Patrick Mahomes has built a successful career with the Kansas City Chiefs. The quarterback has invested in several businesses and sports teams. Mahomes discussed the lessons he has picked up while building his business portfolio. His godfather, former MLB pitcher LaTroy Hawkins, and his teammate and close friend Travis Kelce have influenced his approach.

Travis Kelce’s $5.35 million Ohio mansion has become the centre of a growing neighborhood dispute, with concerns about privacy, property boundaries and the look of the lakefront estate complicating his plans. The Kansas City Chiefs star has faced fresh resistance from residents in Bratenahl, where local officials have approved parts of the proposed landscaping but rejected other elements. Despite efforts to address objections, the project remains unfinished, forcing Kelce’s team to revisit its plans as tensions with longtime neighbors continue to simmer.The dispute surrounding Travis Kelce’s luxury property has taken another turn after a village review board declined to approve trees proposed along the shoreline. Officials also placed conditions on parts of the front landscaping, leaving the project with more work to complete before the estate’s outdoor plans can move forward.Kelce’s property in Bratenahl, near Cleveland, spans approximately 21,000 square feet and includes eight bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, a guest cottage, a swimming pool and a converted ballroom and game room. The scale of the estate has brought added attention to plans for privacy and landscaping in the established lakeside community.The proposed six-foot aluminum fence has also drawn objections. Residents raised concerns about its appearance, its potential effect on wildlife and whether it would provide meaningful protection from unwanted attention. One neighbor warned that deer could become trapped on the fence’s pointed tops.The review process has highlighted the challenge of balancing a high-profile homeowner’s security needs with local rules designed to protect lake views, neighborhood character and property values.Sewer infrastructure remains one of the concerns raised by neighboring residents, but it is not the only issue holding up the project.Katherine Bolton, who has lived next door for 35 years, questioned plans to plant around 50 evergreen trees near an old clay sewer line. She said the roots could cause serious damage and cited a potential $75,000 repair bill for lining the pipe.“Planting 50 evergreen trees just ten feet from a 100-year-old clay sewer line is virtually guaranteed to cause severe root intrusion, pipe structural failure, and catastrophic sewage backups,” she said, citing AI-based research.Kelce’s construction team has pushed back by pointing to changes made in response to residents’ complaints. Project representative Jacob Kutz said the owners had already paid $7,500 to repair a damaged section of the sewer line without seeking contributions from the neighbors.The team also moved the fence two feet inside the property boundary, added access gates and paid to trim trees on neighboring land.Those adjustments have not resolved every disagreement. The board has allowed some landscaping work but wants a revised proposal for the shoreline trees.For Kelce, the next step is to return with a plan that addresses the remaining objections while meeting the village’s requirements. Until then, the mansion’s landscaping project remains caught between private property plans and the expectations of the surrounding community.

Concerns about privacy, property boundaries and the look of the lakefront estate complicating his plans. The Kansas City Chiefs star has faced fresh resistance from residents in Bratenahl, where local officials have approved parts of the proposed landscaping.

Article Title: “It's a family": Travis Kelce makes emotional admission about Patrick Mahomes as Chiefs chase another Super Bowl title

Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce reveal the secret behind their connection

Winning three Super Bowl titles together has given Travis Kelce and Patrick Mahomes plenty to celebrate, but their bond goes beyond touchdowns and championship rings. As the Kansas City Chiefs prepare for their Week 7 clash with the Seattle Seahawks, Kelce has offered insight into what makes the team so difficult to beat. For the veteran tight end, success starts with trust, respect and a shared sense of belonging. His comments also highlight why the partnership between him and Mahomes remains central to Kansas City's ambitions as the team looks to extend its perfect start to the 2026 season.The Chiefs entered Week 7 with an unbeaten 5-0 record, and Kelce believes the atmosphere inside the organisation plays a major role in that success. Speaking with Mahomes during an interview with Chris Berman, the 37-year-old tight end described a culture that encourages players to support one another and compete for a common goal.“It's a family from the top down,” Kelce said.He explained how that connection can make a difference when the pressure rises during a game.“And the culture, that chemistry you build because it's a family environment — you love the guy even more, you're going to do everything you can to get the job done because of how much you respect that dude and that guy for doing the exact same thing.And on top of that, you gotta have fun while doing it.”For Kelce, the Chiefs' winning environment is built on more than individual talent. Players who trust their teammates are more willing to make sacrifices, stay committed and work through difficult moments together.That philosophy has helped Kansas City remain a major force in the NFL . Kelce and Mahomes have connected for 773 receptions, 9,222 receiving yards and 63 touchdowns across 128 regular-season and postseason games.The relationship between Kelce and Mahomes offers a clear example of the communication that drives the Chiefs' offence. Their understanding developed through countless conversations, practice sessions and shared experiences on the field.Kelce credited his quarterback with helping him reach another level as a player.“My game sure as hell skyrocketed and went up when he got here because his football intelligence and his ability to see the game is like none other.”Mahomes has also explained how their partnership began to take shape in 2018, when he became Kansas City's starting quarterback. After each series during training camp, Kelce would ask what Mahomes had noticed and why he had chosen particular throws.“It started in training camp that first year I was starting, after every series he would ask me what I was seeing, why I wanted to throw it here,” Mahomes said. “Through those conversations, I started understanding what he was seeing. Now he's able to do a lot of freelancing in the offense because we are on the same page.”That early investment in communication continues to pay dividends. With Kansas City chasing another championship, the connection between its star quarterback and veteran tight end remains one of the team's biggest strengths.

Article Title: D Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov: What do world's top GMs think about the upcoming World Chess Championship match?
Article Text:
Geneva is set for Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov encounter

'Sometimes it all comes down to one move': Nepo

Ian Nepomniachtchi’s World Chess Championship Insight

'I expect Gukesh to be in a fighting mood': Aronian

Levon Aronian on World Championship Pressure

'Chess is a highly psychological game': Carlsen

Magnus Carlsen shares his opinion

'Gukesh needs to arrive with a positive mindset': MVL

MVL makes World Championship prediction

'Gukesh has enough time to regain his form': Wei Yi

Wei Yi on upcoming World C'ship match

'A real battle of minds between the two players'

S​rinath Narayanan on Gukesh's state after Olympiad 2026​

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A pressure cooker may seem like a less flamboyant invention these days, especially with Elon Musk’s “flying cars” making the rounds on the internet. Yet, it remains a fascinating feat of human-led engineering, built on a simple principle of physics. Seal the vessel, trap the heat, and raise the internal pressure to allow temperatures that ordinary atmospheric conditions would not permit.In sports, defending a world title can have a similar effect on the human mind, can't it?When you are chasing a championship, every win feels like free money. But once the lid seals and you’re holding the crown, every draw feels like a defense, every loss feels like a crisis, and the pressure cooker turns on.That psychological pressure cooker is the backdrop for next month’s World Championship match in Geneva.India's Dommaraju Gukesh is that young champion struggling to rediscover his peak form. Meanwhile, 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov enters with maximum momentum after tearing through the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus.Outwardly, it looks like a battle between a confident challenger and a champion under siege.But is there more to it? With less than a month remaining for the mega encounter, TimesofIndia.com today looks at what the world’s top grandmasters think about the 14-game duel ahead."They always say that match is very different to normal tournaments and that's true," former World Championship challenger and current Russian No. 1 Ian Nepomniachtchi told this website . "But if we see Gukesh's progress for the past like couple of years I believe is pretty much negative. I don't know what happened to him, honestly. And as for now, I think Sindarov is of course a clear favourite."Nepomniachtchi feels that Gukesh’s last truly commanding performance was at Wijk aan Zee in early 2025, where he finished tied for first with fellow Indian Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa but lost the title on tiebreak. After that, it has been abysmal.Nevertheless, Nepo, now 36, also knows firsthand how quickly a match dynamic can shift once the clocks start ticking."Once again, the match is very special, and if you manage to clinch one win (at the start), then you can sit behind your opening prep," Nepomniachtchi added."I think a good example is the Karjakin-Carlsen match. So no one expected Sergey to be like such a tough opponent for Magnus. But I think Sergey had a very, very fair chance to win... Sometimes it all comes down to one move."That psychological weight of wearing the champion's armour so early in life is something veteran grandmaster Levon Aronian views with deep empathy."Gukesh is a big fighter," Aronian said in an interaction with TimesofIndia.com . "He has been a bit down, but I expect him to be in a fighting mood for the match. Of course, it's tremendous pressure. You know, you're so young and your lifetime dream just came too early. I think the same kind of thing happened to Mikhail Tal. He also became a world champion too early. And of course, it's normal to be overwhelmed."At the moment, people think that Gukesh is going to go and try to be very cautious, like in a similar style to how Ding (Liren) was doing against Nepomniachtchi, or also the way Ding was playing against Gukesh as well," Aronian remarked. "There are so many choices to make, and it's definitely going to be an interesting match from a strategical point. I expect Sindarov to be continuing playing very interesting chess the way he's doing. "While Sindarov arrives with wind in his sails, five-time World Champion Magnus Carlsen believes the framing around Gukesh’s mindset needs a complete reset."The word 'defend' is really not a good place to begin, because in terms of how Gukesh has played for the last couple of years, he should not be in a position where he has to defend anything," Carlsen, when asked about Gukesh's chances of defending the World Championship crown, explained . "He should be in a position where he has everything to gain."Emphasising that classical matches are deeply psychological, Carlsen also feels a single shift in momentum can completely rewrite expectations."He (Gukesh) has shown previously in 2024 that when things click, he has the potential to play at an extremely high level," the current World No. 1 added. "I don't think a lot of people believe that he will do it now, but I think it's even more of an interesting challenge for him to try and get back to that. Chess is a highly psychological game, so it probably won't take a lot to potentially place some doubts in Sindarov's mind and some confidence for Gukesh. "Carlsen's sentiment was echoed by French grandmaster Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, who senses that while Sindarov brings stability and form, Gukesh holds the key to how the match actually unfolds."From Sindarov’s point of view, I think it’s clear that this year he has been quite successful," MVL told TimesofIndia.com . "He has been very clutch, very calm, and very determined. So, he is not the variable. Gukesh is the variable."Fresh off the Chess Olympiad, where Gukesh won two silver medals, 36-year-old MVL believes the Samarkand experience could well turn the tide for the Indian grandmaster."I think, of course, all the talk is about how Gukesh has been struggling over the past few months," MVL remarked. "And I do think he needs to arrive with a positive mindset because, chess-wise, if he plays at his best level, he is at least as good as Sindarov. Gukesh has been playing extremely well in the past two Olympiads. If he can use that to play well again, maybe this will be the way for him to get into a positive mindset before the match. "China's top-ranked player, Wei Yi, who competed alongside Sindarov in Cyprus, cautioned against writing off the reigning champion based purely on recent rating points."Yes, I also participated in the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus earlier this year," Wei told TimesofIndia.com "We all know that Sindarov ultimately won the tournament. He performed extremely well and secured first place with a commanding lead, clinching the title ahead of the final round. However, some people may feel that Gukesh has not been in particularly good form recently, and his rating has been declining. If he continues in this form, they might expect the World Championship match to be one-sided, with Sindarov winning comfortably. But I don't think it will be that simple, because there is still time before the match. I believe Gukesh has enough time to regain his form, and I'm sure he has already started preparing."Wei pointed to a crucial factor that rating algorithms often miss."I believe experience will be extremely important in a contest like this," Wei added. "The World Championship match is different from any other tournament. Two players are fighting for the highest title in chess, and they have to face the same opponent over nearly a month, constantly thinking about how to defeat them. I think experience will certainly matter, and Gukesh clearly has an advantage in that respect."Giving an update on Gukesh's mentality after this Olympiad, GM Srinath Narayanan, who captained the Indian team in the open section at this 2026 Samarkand Olympiad , agreed that the unique format of match play acts as a great equaliser."I think Gukesh is in a much better mental space after the Olympiad, because it was probably his first really good tournament in a long time," Srinath told this website. "It will be close, not as one-sided as what the ratings reflect. Javokhir enters with a lot of confidence, and that can change if there's an early good result for Gukesh."Srinath noted that while Sindarov's opening preparation has looked formidable in recent months, but it will not matter much when he sits in Geneva later next month."He's also showing an incredible amount of opening preparation against other opponents, but in a World Championship match, this gets neutralised," Srinath remarked. "Both players see everything the other has. There are factors going Javokhir's way right now, but they can even out over a match. I think it's going to be a very close, very interesting one.""I think it will be a close match probably," Alireza Firouzja noted , keeping it short. "Anything could happen."If anything, Geneva will not merely test engine lines and endgame technique, as Wei Yi concluded, "Personally, it will be a very close match. I can't say for certain who will win, but regardless of who I think might win or who I want to win, I hope we get to see a fantastic contest, a real battle of minds between the two players."
Article Summary: India's Dommaraju Gukesh is struggling to rediscover his peak form. 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov enters with maximum momentum after tearing through the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus. Former World Championship challenger and current Russian No. 1 Ian Nepomniachtchi says Sindarov is a clear favourite.

Pakistan book a place in the final

NEW DELHI: For a few moments at Lahore's Gaddafi Stadium, it seemed Pakistan had lost the match. England's players had started celebrating, handshakes were exchanged and Shadab Khan looked devastated. But a review changed everything, and the hosts went on to pull off a stunning one-wicket victory in the ODI tri-series on Sunday.Pakistan were chasing 242 and had slipped to 154-9. With just one wicket left, defeat looked certain. Then Shadab and Haris Rauf produced a remarkable fightback, taking Pakistan home and securing their place in the final.Shadab remained unbeaten on 113, but his innings had one moment that could have ended the contest before its dramatic finish.The drama unfolded in the 45th over when Gus Atkinson trapped Shadab on the pads. The bowler appealed, and the umpire raised his finger. Shadab appeared to accept his fate and began walking away.England's players thought they had won. Some started shaking hands, while the television briefly flashed a result showing England winning by 20 runs.Shadab was clearly upset. He struck his bat against the ground and went down on his haunches. Joe Root and Harry Brook approached him to shake hands as other England players began celebrating.But Shadab decided to review the decision, and the replays changed the mood inside the stadium. UltraEdge showed a spike, confirming that the ball had touched his bat before hitting his pad.The decision was overturned, and the crowd erupted. Shadab was given another chance to finish the match, while England's players looked stunned. Rauf, who had put his hand on his head during the tense moment, also watched in disbelief.Shadab responded with a fist pump. Pakistan's hopes were alive again, and the match continued.When Rauf joined Shadab in the 34th over, Pakistan were struggling at 154-9. England needed only one more wicket, but the last pair refused to surrender.Shadab took responsibility for the chase, scoring quickly and protecting Rauf from facing too many deliveries. He kept most of the strike and continued to put pressure on England's bowlers.Playing his first match of the tournament, Shadab smashed 113 not out off 96 balls, with 12 fours and five sixes. Rauf supported him with an unbeaten seven off 19 deliveries.Their 89-run partnership was the highest for the 10th wicket in a successful ODI run chase.Shadab brought up his maiden ODI century with a late cut off Atkinson and followed it with a six over long-off. Pakistan needed only three runs from the final three overs when Rauf struck the winning boundary off Henry Crocombe.Pakistan finished on 243-9 in 47.1 overs to complete a victory few would have expected when their ninth wicket fell.Earlier, England were dismissed for 241 in 46.4 overs after being asked to bat first. Ben Duckett top-scored with 105 off 111 balls, hitting 10 fours and two sixes.Shaheen Shah Afridi put England under pressure from the start. He dismissed Tom Banton in the first over and Joe Root in the third, before Rauf removed Jordan Cox. England were soon reduced to 52-4.Duckett and Sam Curran then gave the innings some stability, adding 93 runs for the fifth wicket. Curran scored 42 off 52 balls before Afridi dismissed him, completing his third wicket of the innings.Afridi finished with 4-46 as England continued to lose wickets. They slipped to 201-9 before Gus Atkinson, who remained unbeaten on 36, helped them reach 241.Despite Duckett's century and Atkinson's late contribution, England's total was not enough to stop Pakistan's remarkable chase.Pakistan also struggled with the bat. Fakhar Zaman and Babar Azam scored 10 each, while Saim Ayub managed only six. Jamie Overton took two catches in the slips to dismiss Fakhar and Saim, while Atkinson bowled Babar.Saad Baig added a quick 32 off 22 balls, and Salman Ali Agha scored 26. But England continued to take wickets, with Overton finishing with 3-43 and Liam Dawson claiming 2-30.At 154-9, England were firmly in control. However, Shadab's counter-attack, Rauf's support and the crucial review turned the match on its head.The victory secured Pakistan's place in the ODI tri-series final. They will play Sri Lanka in their last league match on Tuesday, having beaten them by 37 runs in the opening game.England, meanwhile, suffered their third consecutive defeat. They had earlier lost to Pakistan by 87 runs and then suffered a heartbreaking loss against Sri Lanka, who chased down 430 with one ball remaining.
Article Summary: Pakistan beat England by one wicket to book place in final of ODI tri-series. England bowled out for 241 in 46.4 overs after being asked to bat first. Ben Duckett top scored with 105 off 111 balls, hitting 10 fours and two sixes.

NEW DELHI: Devdutt Padikkal was left heartbroken after missing out on a double century by just one run on Day 3 of the first unofficial Test between India A and New Zealand A at the Bert Sutcliffe Oval in Lincoln.The left-hander looked shocked when umpire raised his finger after New Zealand A appealed for a catch behind off Zak Gibson. Padikkal stood on the pitch for a few moments, looking at the umpire and signalling that the ball had gone down the leg side and appeared to have brushed his pads.But the decision went against him, forcing him to walk back to the pavilion on 199. The ball appeared to brush his pads before settling into wicketkeeper Mitchell Hay's gloves. There was a sound as the ball passed the bat, but Padikkal seemed convinced that it had not come off his bat. The appeal did not appear particularly strong, yet the umpire raised his finger.Padikkal immediately looked towards the umpire in disbelief and gestured to show how far the ball was from his bat.He remained on the pitch briefly, clearly unhappy with the decision, before making his way back.His innings ended at 199 off 248 balls, including 24 fours and three sixes. It was a fine knock under pressure, but the manner and timing of his dismissal made the end particularly painful.India A had been bowled out for just 113 in the first innings and needed a strong response. However, their openers failed again, with Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul falling early in the second innings. India A were reduced to 10 for two, leaving the team in trouble once more.Padikkal then took charge and helped India A recover from the early collapse.

Article Title: Back to the classroom: Nearly 7 lakh elders take literacy test across Maharashtra
Article Text:
On Sunday, nearly seven lakh elderly individuals participated in the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Test in Maharashtra (Photo credit: Prasad Joshi)

Mangal Baban Mane, in yellow sari, writes the exam in one of the exam centres in Kolhapur (Photo credit: Kolhapur Municipal Corporation)

One of the exam centres in Kolhapur

For many elders, achievement was just writing test





CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR/KOLHAPUR/NASHIK: A grandson taught his grandmother her first letters. Another proudly accompanied his grandfather to an exam. On Sunday, together, they turned a literacy test into a celebration of second chances.65-year-old Mangal Baban Mane of Kolhapur once dreamt of becoming a govt officer. Life had other plans. Poverty and circumstances cut short her education.On Sunday, decades later, she took her seat for Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Test (FLNAT), carrying with her lessons taught not by a teacher, but by her grandson.“My grandson is in Class V. He taught me Marathi letters and helped me learn words. He also taught me counting from one to 100,” Mane said. “Now I can do basic addition and subtraction. Most importantly, I can write my own name.”Hundreds of kilometres away in Nashik, science graduate Shashank Borse proudly escorted his 68-year-old grandfather to another examination centre.The older man had spent his life in the fields so that future generations could study. On Sunday, it was his turn to become the student.Together, their stories captured the spirit of a remarkable statewide exercise that saw nearly seven lakh elderly learners appear for FLNAT under the ULLAS (Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society) programme of New India Literacy Programme (NILP).For Vimal Kanu, 60, from Satara’s Man taluka, the examination marked another milestone in a journey of self-belief. She had appeared last year but did not clear the test. This time, she walked into the classroom with confidence.“The change in my life is visible,” she said. “Earlier, I used a thumb impression. Now I sign my name. I can read small words and understand what is written. I can even check whether a shopkeeper has returned the correct balance,” she added.Across Maharashtra , elderly men and women who had missed out on schooling decades ago returned to classrooms, many writing their first formal examination.The test, conducted in nine languages, including Marathi, Hindi, English and Urdu, is part of govt’s effort to bring non-literate adults into the education system.“Around seven lakh learners registered on the ULLAS app appeared for the examination. Those who qualify can continue their education through standards three, five, eight, 10 and 12 equivalents,” said education director (planning) Krishnakumar Patil.“He spent his youth working on the farm so the generations after him could study,” Borse said of his grandfather.“Because of his sacrifices, my father became a teacher and I found a job in Nashik. Taking him to this exam was one of the proudest moments of our lives. He is the only one among seven siblings who dared to take the test. I hope others now follow him,” Borse said.The response was especially strong in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, where more than 41,000 candidates appeared at 2,698 centres. Against a target of 47,368 learners, 43,700 had registered for the programme.Officials said the initiative extends beyond literacy.“Through FLNAT, we aim to build financial, legal and digital literacy, along with health awareness and other life skills that help improve quality of life,” Patil said.The scale of the literacy drive came alive at the Dhoregaon cluster, where 198 neo-literates turned up to write the test at Zilla Parishad Central Primary School and its satellite centres.Guided by centre head Sachin Damale, in-charge headmaster Rajesh Hiwale and a team of teachers, the centres transformed into classrooms of second chances as elderly learners, many writing an examination for the first time in their lives, took their seats with quiet determination.“They were welcomed with flowers before the exam,” said Hiwale. “The welcome eased their fears and boosted their confidence. The most memorable sight was seeing elderly learners arrive with their grandchildren, who watched with pride as their grandparents read, wrote and solved questions on their own.”The examination carried 150 marks and required a minimum score of 33%.For many candidates, however, the day’s biggest achievement was not the result that will arrive later. It was simply walking into a classroom, taking a seat and writing the test.
Article Summary: Nearly seven lakh elderly individuals participated in the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Test in Maharashtra. The test, conducted in nine languages, including Marathi, Hindi, English and Urdu, is part of govt’s effort to bring non-literate adults into the education system.

Article Title: Cheered in Chhota Udepur, but Vadodara shuts stage to Muslim who played Lakshmana for 14 years
Article Text:
Abid Sheikh, an actor in Vadodara, was excluded from performing in Ram Leela due to his religion.





VADODARA: On Dussehra , Abid Sheikh drew applause in tribal Chhota Udepur for bringing the characters of Kevat and Meghnad alive on stage in a Ram Leela.In Vadodara, however, the city he calls home, the 39-year-old was unable to perform in the Ram Leela he had been associated with for nearly 14 years, after objections to his participation over his religion by right-wing groups.The contrast has left Sheikh, a science graduate who grew up fascinated by the Ramayana, grappling with an unexpected rejection from a tradition that had become an integral part of his life.For years, Sheikh played Laxman and Bharat in the Ram Leela organised by the North India Cultural Association (NICA) at Polo Ground during Dussehra. He learnt his dialogues, rehearsed for weeks and earned appreciation from audiences. His family, too, shared his commitment, giving up non-vegetarian food during the rehearsal period until the festival concluded.But the welcome he had long received on stage in Vadodara changed last year when some right-wing activists turned up during rehearsals and objected to his casting because he was a Muslim.“I played different roles in Ram Leela for around 14 years and was showered with love and appreciation by the audience.Last year, some activists suddenly turned up during rehearsals and objected to my casting because of my religion. I was shocked, as I never expected this,” Sheikh told TOI.He said the activists pressured the organisers to drop him. This year, he was not invited to perform in the Vadodara production.“Ram Leela had become a part of my life, but they did not want me anywhere near the stage,” he said.The rejection was particularly painful because his association with the epic began in childhood. After watching a cartoon based on the Ramayana, Sheikh developed a fascination for Laxman. An opportunity to perform in a school Ram Leela gave him his first taste of acting, and he continued playing characters from the epic for years.Shashikant Das, director, NICA, told TOI: “Sheikh is such a good actor and he is an ardent fan of Ramayan. He chants Hanuman Chalisa. But Bajrang Dal activists came last year and protested against his role. I argued and fought in Sheikh’s defence.”“But the management came under pressure. So, this time he wasn’t invited for the Ram Leela. It’s sad that we lost a good actor like him,” Das said and pointed out that those preparing the giant effigies of Ravana, Meghnad and Kumbhakarna at Polo Ground are also Muslim artists from Uttar Pradesh.
Article Summary: Abid Sheikh, an actor in Vadodara, was excluded from performing in Ram Leela due to his religion. Right-wing activists turned up during rehearsals and objected to his casting because he was a Muslim. He said the activists pressured the organisers to drop him.

Article Title: 'I genuinely thought I was going to die': Ex-Australia cricketer Usman Khawaja reveals career-long health secret
Article Text:
Australia's Usman Khawaja (Reuters/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

Why Khawaja kept his illness secret

Khawaja's cricket career and lasting message

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sabr

Former Australia opener Usman Khawaja has revealed that he battled rheumatoid arthritis throughout his international cricket career, keeping the condition hidden from his teammates for years.Speaking on ABC, the 39-year-old recalled being diagnosed with the illness at just 22, when severe pain in his left knee made even walking difficult.“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” Khawaja said, describing how he went from being an athletic cricketer to someone who could barely walk 10 metres.He was diagnosed in 2009 while playing for New South Wales during the off-season. Although doctors and cricket officials knew about his condition, he chose not to tell his teammates.Khawaja feared that revealing his health problems could be used against him, and he did not want people treating him differently. As a result, even former teammates David Warner and Michael Hussey were unaware of his condition.He relied on regular medication and injections to control the disease and returned to cricket around six months after his diagnosis. The treatment played a crucial role in helping him continue his career."Without that drug, I would never have played cricket ever again or even lived a normal life again,” he said.Khawaja hopes his experience will encourage people living with autoimmune diseases to keep pursuing their goals.“If a person can play at the top level as a professional cricketer with rheumatoid arthritis, then I think a lot of other people can achieve a lot, too,” he added.Khawaja made his Test debut against England at the Sydney Cricket Ground in January 2011. Despite being dropped from the team several times, he made important comebacks. One of his biggest achievements came during the 2021-22 Ashes, when he scored centuries in both innings of the Sydney Test.He retired from Test cricket in January 2026 after the fifth Ashes Test against England in Sydney. He finished with 6,229 runs and 16 centuries in 88 Tests.Khawaja is also preparing to share more about his life and career in his upcoming autobiography,His story highlights the health struggles that can exist behind the success of professional athletes. By speaking publicly about his illness after retirement, Khawaja hopes to raise awareness about rheumatoid arthritis and show others that a chronic condition does not necessarily mean giving up on their ambitions.
Article Summary: Usman Khawaja has revealed he battled rheumatoid arthritis throughout his international cricket career. The 39-year-old was diagnosed with the illness at just 22, when severe pain in his left knee made even walking difficult. He kept the condition hidden from his teammates for years, fearing it could be used against him.
